problem: LLMs asked to write LTL formulas directly often produce syntactically invalid formulas (missing parentheses/operands), and end-to-end LLM planners struggle with long-horizon navigation with temporal constraints. Fine-tuned LTL translators do not scale to complex formulas.
motivation: LTL gives verifiable task constraints that enable optimal, collision-free motion planning, but only if the formula is syntactically valid and semantically right. LLMs are trained on far more code than temporal logic, so they should be used where they are strong (code writing).
key_idea: Prompt an LLM to write Python code that calls a predefined library of LTL operator functions, so executing the code yields an LTL formula that is syntactically correct by construction.
insight: Syntax correctness comes from routing LTL construction through code, with execution errors fed back for a retry. The ablations show that natural-language explanations in the code matter most: removing them drops GPT-4o Tier 3 success from 100 to 60 and Tier 4 from 70 to 50. Line comments matter little and can even add noise for the smaller model. Model size matters for ambiguous Tier 4 tasks: GPT-4o-mini gets 0% on Tier 4.
method: Semantic occupancy mapping: DLO odometry + YOLO segmentation + SSMI fuse RGB-D/LiDAR into a 3D semantic occupancy map, projected to a 2D map with FREE/NULL/UNKNOWN/object classes; atomic propositions defined by proximity to classes
Object identification: an LLM prompt rewrites the instruction by replacing object names with unique class IDs from the map, to ground symbols

Code generation: few-shot prompt with imported library functions (ap, ltl_and, ltl_or, ltl_not, ltl_until, ltl_eventually, ltl_always, ltl_imply); the LLM writes an explanation, creates atomic propositions, composes operators, and returns the LTL formula (implementations hidden)
Syntax check loop: the generated code is executed; on error the previous code and failure reason are fed back for a retry

Planning: LTL to Büchi automaton (Spot); product graph over 8-connected map cells and automaton states; A* with a consistent LTL heuristic (from NL2LTL) yields a collision-free path, tracked by a controller

setting.training_data: none (training-free; few-shot prompts with 5-20 examples per dataset)
setting.observation: RGB-D / range sensor, semantic occupancy map built beforehand by exploration
setting.action_space: 8-direction grid path in a 2D semantic occupancy map, tracked by a controller on a Jackal ground robot
setting.simulator: none for navigation (GTB 2D grid maps); real-world mock indoor environment
setting.privileged: Pre-built semantic occupancy map from prior exploration/teleoperation (GTB uses given maps)

numbers.extra: few-shot prompting; compared with GPT-4o end-to-end planner (7.84 acc)
numbers.evidence: Table 2: GTB evaluation; Ours 78.91 accuracy, 82.49 MPL

numbers.eval_set_note: Tier 1: 10, Tier 2: 10, Tier 3: 15, Tier 4: 10 scenarios; success per tier
numbers.extra: success rate by tier; syntactic failure 0 in all tiers; LLM runtime 7.07±4.31 s

numbers.eval_set_note: Drone, Cleanup, Pick datasets, human-written and synthetic instructions

numbers_note: No standard VLN/ObjNav benchmarks; navigation evaluated on GTB and 45 real-world tasks. Real-world tier numbers are success rates per tier.
results: LTLCodeGen reaches 98.9-99.9% LTL translation accuracy on Drone/Cleanup/Pick, beating NL2LTL (95.2-98.7) and fine-tuned BART. On GTB it gets 78.91% accuracy vs 7.84% for the end-to-end GPT-4o planner. In real-world tasks it has zero syntactic errors and outperforms NL2LTL on Tier 3 (100 vs 46.7).
limitations: Semantic errors on ambiguous, context-dependent instructions (Tier 4: 70% with GPT-4o, 0% with GPT-4o-mini)
Slower LLM inference than NL2LTL (7.07 s vs 2.01 s) because full code with explanations is generated
Planner fails when the generated LTL is unsatisfiable in the map (e.g., an objective requires passing through a later one); needs a pre-built semantic map
